Medical History

- Current health issues and chronic disease risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes):  Painful, cracked, itchy skin on palms for 3–4 months; Type 2 diabetes mellitus; baseline dry skin (legs) mild.
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes):  Diabetes; no known family history of skin disease, asthma, or bowel disease.
- Current medications including OTC and traditional medicines:  Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented); OTC emollient “E45” previously tried without benefit; oral antihistamine previously tried without benefit; topical corticosteroid cream prescribed today (name/dose/route/frequency not documented); stronger emollient advised 3–4 times daily for 10–14 days.
- Immunisation status reviewed (flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal, shingles, tetanus):  Not recorded.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Summary of key clinical findings:  3–4 months of painful, fissured, itchy palmar dermatitis with intermittent bleeding only after scratching. Occupational exposure to cleaning chemicals; inconsistent glove use. Baseline xerosis (legs). No systemic symptoms. Type 2 diabetes. No known allergies.
- Working diagnosis:  Irritant contact hand dermatitis due to occupational exposure to cleaning products and wet work, supported by strong temporal association with new hotel housekeeping job, palmar-dominant fissuring/itch/pain, lack of response to antihistamines, and inadequate glove use (consistent with DDx).
- Considerations (from DDx, plausible but uncertain):  Allergic contact dermatitis to cleaning agents/glove components; Asteatotic/xerotic eczema (barrier dysfunction) exacerbated by diabetes and frequent washing. Lower-likelihood alternatives (not primary): dyshidrotic eczema, tinea manuum.
- Plan:
  - Trigger avoidance: Wear protective gloves consistently for all cleaning tasks; minimize wet work and harsh chemical exposure.
  - Skin care: Begin prescribed topical corticosteroid cream (specific potency/regimen not documented); apply stronger emollient liberally 3–4 times daily for 10–14 days.
  - Safety-netting: Return in 10–14 days if not improved; earlier if worsening or spreading.
  - Follow-up for diabetes and skin healing considerations is advisable; no labs or additional investigations recorded today.

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification:  Education provided on trigger avoidance and consistent glove use; frequent moisturization emphasized to restore skin barrier.

- Irritant contact hand dermatitis (High): Strong temporal link to new housekeeping job, frequent chemical exposure and wet work with inconsistent glove use; palmar fissuring, pain, and itch.
- Allergic contact dermatitis (Medium): Possible sensitization to cleaning agents or glove components; pruritic chronic hand dermatitis could be mixed irritant/allergic.
- Asteatotic/xerotic eczema (Medium): Baseline generalized dryness and diabetes-related xerosis may contribute to barrier dysfunction and fissuring.
